deep.reconstruction:
The page is the first worked example for the 'analyseur' set up on the previous page. There, an analyseur is a k0-algebra Ω0 that also has an associative composition F∘G with unit T, and composition on the right by a fixed G is a k0-algebra homomorphism. In modern terms this is a plethory, a monoid in birings in the sense of Tall–Wraith and Borger–Wieland. Here k0 = Z.

(1) Basis. Grothendieck introduces the binomial polynomials F_n(T) = T(T−1)…(T−n+1)/n! = C(T,n) in Q[T]. They span ⊕_n Z·F_n inside Q[T], which is the ring Int(Z) of integer-valued polynomials.

(2) Product. He writes the multiplication table (*): F_m F_n = Σ_p c^p_{m,n} F_p, with c^p_{m,n} ∈ Z. Nonzero terms occur only for max(m,n) ≤ p ≤ m+n.

(3) Composition. He writes F_m(F_n(T)) = Σ_{0≤p≤mn} d^p_{m,n} F_p(T). The coefficients are implicitly integers, since a composite of integer-valued polynomials is integer-valued and the F_p form a Z-basis. So ⊕ Z F_n is stable under ∘.

(4) Presentation. ⊕ Z F_n ⊂ Q[T] is described as the commutative unital Z-algebra generated by the F_n subject to F_0 = 1 and the relations (*), with F_1 = T. This is a tautological presentation: the F_n form a basis and (*) is the full multiplication table.

(5) Additive co-operation. F_m(P+Q) = Σ δ^m_{ij} F_i(P) F_j(Q). This is the Vandermonde identity, so δ^m_{ij} = 1 if i+j = m and 0 otherwise. It defines a coaddition δ: Ω → Ω ⊗_Z Ω, F ↦ F(X+Y).

(6) Multiplicative co-operation. He begins F_m(PQ) = Σ … (left unfinished). It encodes the comultiplication F ↦ F(XY), for which C(xy,m) is an integral combination of C(x,i)C(y,j).

(7) Pointwise form and generality. 'F_m(x+y), F_m(xy)' restates the same identities pointwise. 'Σ a_i T^i, a_i ∈ Q' points to the general setting developed on the next page: Ω = {F ∈ K0[T] : F(k0) ⊂ k0}. There, coaddition and comultiplication land in Ω⊗Ω when Ω is free over k0.

Purpose: to exhibit Int(Z), the ring of numerical polynomials, as the basic example of an analyseur/plethory over Z. Its 'algebras' (the structures acting on rings, via W(A) on the previous page) would be binomial rings.
errors: No mathematical error. The presentation 'generated by F_n with relations F_0=1 and (*)' is correct but tautological, since the F_n are a Z-basis and (*) is the full multiplication table.
The sum range 0≤p≤m+n in (*) is correct but loose: c^p_{m,n}=0 for p<max(m,n).
The formula for F_m(P(T)Q(T)) is left incomplete; the right-hand side should be Σ μ^m_{ij} F_i(P)F_j(Q).

ideas.what: Binomial polynomials C(T,n) as a Z-basis of the integer-valued polynomial ring
ideas.modern_name: Int(Z) = ring of numerical polynomials, Pólya basis
ideas.where_published: Numerical polynomials appear in Grothendieck's Riemann–Roch work (SGA 6 milieu)

ideas.what: Integral structure constants for product and composition of binomial polynomials; Int(Z) closed under composition
ideas.modern_name: Int(Z) as a composition ring / plethory

ideas.what: Coaddition δ: Ω→Ω⊗Ω via F(X+Y) (Vandermonde) and comultiplication via F(XY), making Int(Z) a co-ring object
ideas.modern_name: Biring structure on Int(Z) representing the identity functor on binomial rings

ideas.what: The general notion of 'analyseur' (algebra with associative composition, right composition being an algebra map, acting on W(A))

missed.claim: Around 1982 Grothendieck independently formulated what is now called a plethory ('analyseur'), with integer-valued polynomials as the first worked example, including coaddition and comultiplication. This anticipates Borger–Wieland (2005) and Elliott's (2006) treatment of Int(Z) as a plethory whose algebras are binomial rings. Tall–Wraith (1970) had the abstract notion earlier, so this is a historical rather than mathematical priority point.
missed.quote: ⊕ Z.F_n ⊂ Q[T] est la Z-algèbre comm. unit. engendrée par les F_n … ; δ : Ω → Ω⊗_Z Ω
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It documents Grothendieck's unknown interest in plethystic algebra and Witt-type functors (W(A) on the previous page). That is relevant to the history of 'F_1 / Λ-geometry' (Borger), where Int(Z) and Witt vectors play central roles.

missed.claim: The multiplicative co-operation F_m(xy) = Σ μ^m_{ij} F_i(x)F_j(y) is begun but not completed. The general framework, Ω = {F ∈ K0[T] : F(k0) ⊂ k0} for arbitrary k0 ⊂ K0, is pursued on the next page.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Minor: these coefficients are classical. The general 'analyseur of integer-valued polynomials over k0' parallels later work on Int(D) as plethories (Elliott).

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics is classical: Vandermonde, Pólya basis, Int(Z) closed under composition. The notable point is historical: Grothendieck working on plethories ('analyseurs') with Int(Z) as the model example, decades before Borger–Wieland and Elliott made this standard. The Tall–Wraith (1970) precedent keeps the surprise moderate.
transcription_corrections: Under c^p_{m,n} the symbol read as 'Ẑ' is more likely an arrow '^' pointing up to the coefficients with 'Z' below, i.e. 'c^p_{m,n} ∈ Z'.
The insertion over 'Z-algèbre' reads 'comm. unit.', i.e. commutative unital.
Line reads 'F_m(P(T)+Q(T)) = Σ δ^m_{ij} F_i(P(T)) F_j(Q(T))'; the final factor is F_j(Q(T)).
